newsitem.title: USA: Apple Chairman Amelio resigns, Jobs to expand role.
newsitem.headline: Apple Chairman Amelio resigns, Jobs to expand role.

text.p: Gilbert Amelio, the man who was supposed to revive Apple Computer Inc., announced his resignation Wednesday, raising the possibility that ousted co-founder Steven Jobs could once again lead the struggling computer maker.
Apple said the board of directors was unhappy with the company's performance under Amelio, who took over 17 months ago.

"We recognize a lot has been accomplished in the last year and a half under Gil's tenure" said Chief Financial Officer Fred Anderson. "But the fact is we're not yet on a growth path and we haven't returned the company to sustainable profitability."

Since Amelio arrived at Apple in February 1996, Apple has gone through two massive restructurings, fired thousands of employees, replaced its entire suite of senior executives and discontinued several unprofitible products.

But the company has bled red ink every quarter, except for one, losing $1.6 billion over the past six quarters. Its revenue is expected to shrink to about $8.5 billion in the latest fiscal year from $11.1 billion in fiscal 1995.

While Amelio had won some praise for quickly shoring up Apple's weak finances upon his arrival, customers and investors criticized him for failing to come up with a strategy that would stave off the popularity of personal computers based on Microsoft Corp. and Intel Corp. technology.
"Amelio underestimated the extent of the problems at Apple when he got there," said David Wu, analyst at investment bank ABN AMRO Chicago Corp.
Added Lou Mazzucchelli, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison: "He needed to fill the role of a visionary leader, which he didn't fit well."

Until a new chief executive is found, Jobs -- who returned in December to advise Amelio -- will assume an expanded role. He will advise executives on product strategy, marketing and business relationships, Anderson said.
Apple executives refused to say whether Jobs is in the running to replace Amelio.
However, analysts said Jobs, who founded Apple with Stephen Wozniak more than 20 years ago, may find the challenge to run Apple again too hard to resist.
"You can't count Jobs out. He has more lives than a cat," said Tim Bajarin, analyst at market researcher Creative Strategies Research International Corp.
Amelio could not be reached immediately for comment. Jobs, who serves as CEO of Pixar Animation Studios, also could not be reached.

In a letter to shareholders, Jobs recently wrote that Apple's acquisition of Next Software Inc. allows him "to devote all my energy (and hopes and dreams) to the future of Pixar. I am spending all my work life with Pixar and loving it."
Apple said CFO Anderson will handle day-to-day operations while the company searches for a new chief executive.

In a related move, Ellen Hancock, executive vice president of technology, also plans to leave Apple. Amelio had hired Hancock to revamp Apple's aging technology. Her responsibilities have been reassigned to Avie Tevanian and Jon Rubinstein -- two executives who took over Apple's technology development early this year at Jobs' suggestion.

When Amelio came to Apple last year, he had a reputation as a turnaround artist who helped bolster the fortunes of National Semiconductor Corp. He replaced Michael Spindler, an Apple veteran who also was ousted by the board for failing to halt Apple's slide.

Amelio, however, fared no better. Even though Apple's legendary Macintosh computer is regarded by many as the most elegant machine in the industry, the company has been no match for the marketing power of Microsoft and Intel.
"I said when Gil Amelio took over it was a tough job," Wozniak told Reuters in an interview.
Apple's board has had a tough time finding the right leader since 1984.
In 1985, the board ousted Jobs -- who created Apple with Wozniak in Jobs' garage -- over declining financial performance and technology strategy.

John Sculley, a former Pepsi Co. executive, took over. But Sculley fumbled the chance to license Apple's technology to other computer companies, which led Microsoft and Intel to gain market share. He, too, was ousted in 1993.

Investors pinned their hopes on Spindler, who tried to shop Apple around to several companies, including International Business Machines Corp. and Sun Microsystems Inc. As Apple lost more ground to competitors, he failed to find a buyer.
Now, Apple has to find a CEO who can stabilize the company as a smaller niche player, or shape it up so it can be sold to another company, analysts said.

There might still be a buyer for Apple. In April, Larry Ellison, the chairman of database software company Oracle Corp., said he would consider buying Apple with his own money. He said in June he dropped that plan to concentrate on running Oracle.
